h:
Marcion of Sinope. His ideas are still circulating. You’ve probably stumbled on them without knowing it.

Marcion of Sinope was a ship owner’s son from the coast of the Black Sea. He came to Rome around 140 AD with money, influence, and a theology he believed was finally honest about what the New Testament actually taught. He was not a fringe figure muttering at the edges. He was educated, persuasive, and generous enough with his wealth that the Roman church initially received him.

Then they read what he believed.

Marcion of Sinope was declared a heretic in 144 AD. The church spent generations refuting him. He lost the argument.

But he didn’t just lose the theological argument. Polycarp of Smyrna, direct disciple of the Apostle John, encountered him in person.

S. Polycarpus, engraving by Michael Burghers, 1685

Marcion asked Polycarp: “do you know me?”

Polycarp answered: “I know you, the firstborn of Satan.”

Polycarp of Smyrna, the man who chose to burn alive rather than deny the name of Jesus, identified Marcion on sight.

When a man who preferred fire to compromise names your theology, the case is closed before the debate begins.

The modern gnostic teacher denouncing the God of Sinai does it from a comfortable chair, in a temperature-controlled room, with nothing on the line. Polycarp was 86 years old and chose the stake over a single word of compromise.

He knew exactly what he was looking at. His teacher had already named it.

“Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.” - 1 John 2:22

Marcion’s entire logic rested on separating the Father from the Son.

Burning of Polycarp in Smyrna, 155 AD, engraving by Jan Luiken

Seventeen centuries later the theology breathes again, not in dusty gnostic texts, in comment sections, sermon clips, and Substack essays written by people who would recoil at the name Marcion while preaching his conclusions.

The deconstruction space runs on it. Progressive Christianity was built on its bones. And even in conservative evangelical corners, the soft version circulates quietly: the Old Testament as prologue, the Hebrew God as embarrassment, Jesus as the apology.

Nobody hands you a pamphlet. The theology moves by mood. By the way a preacher’s voice drops when he leaves the Gospels and enters Leviticus. By the quiet flinch when you say the God who drowned Pharaoh’s army and the God who raised His Son from the tomb are the same God, unchanged, making the same demand.

You may have seen it here. Dressed in the language of grace. Carrying a cross it has separated from its roots.

That’s Marcion. Without the name tag.

He believed the God of the Old Testament and the Father of Jesus were not the same God. The Hebrew God was lesser. A lawgiver. A Demiurge. Bound to matter and blood and covenant. The true God, in Marcion’s logic, was pure spirit, previously unknown, revealed only in Christ. No history with Abraham. No stake in Israel. No continuity with Moses.

His conclusion was consistent with his premise. He took a knife to the canon. Kept Luke, edited. Kept ten Pauline letters, edited. Threw out everything that contradicted him. Which was most of the New Testament and all of the Old.

This is how you know a system is broken: it can only survive with the evidence removed.

Let the text answer this heresy.

Jesus, Sermon on the Mount:

“Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.” Matthew 5:17.

Jesus did not distance Himself from the Hebrew God. He planted His feet in that tradition and claimed it as His own ground.

Same sermon: “You have heard it said... but I say to you.” Every escalation runs deeper into Torah, not away from it. He’s not overruling Moses. He’s going beneath the surface letter to what the Law always demanded at the bone. The God who said do not murder always meant do not hate. Jesus restores the original intent. He does not replace the Author.

John 5:46: “If you believed Moses, you would believe Me, for he wrote about Me.”

Moses is a witness for Christ. One unbroken testimony.

Paul, whom Marcion claimed as his primary weapon:

Romans 11:29 - “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.”

Paul’s entire argument across Romans 9 through 11 is that the God of Israel has not abandoned Israel, and that this faithfulness is the very ground that makes the gospel trustworthy. If the Hebrew God broke covenant with Israel, you have no reason to trust any promise he made through Christ. Paul knows this. Marcion didn’t.

Hebrews 1:1-2: “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by His Son.”

Marcion’s logic requires you to stop reading before the texts answer him.

When your position only survives inside a shortened canon, you haven’t found a better God. You’ve found a smaller Bible. And you’ve built your house on what was cut, not what was kept.

The Old Testament God who demanded blood on the doorpost in Egypt is the same God whose Son shed blood outside the gates of Jerusalem. The continuity isn’t a problem to explain away. It’s the whole point.

One Author. One narrow and costly redemption line running from Eden to Revelation.

Marcion cut that line and called the wound a door.

It isn’t.

Know them by their fruit.
